maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
When the consideration of this item was postponed at yesterday's sitting I was about to make a few remarks. I did not have an earlier opportunity of speaking on the subject, but having been one of those who sat here during the all-night sitting, and in view of the minister's statement that the greater part of that sitting was devoted to obstruction, it occurred to me that having waited all night for an opportunity to speak I surely ought to intervene in the debate and inform my hon. friend that what he was pleased to call obstruction was simply an effort on the part of hon. gentlemen on this side to secure information and could not in any way be regarded as obstructive tactics.
The few remarks that I intend to offer will be based on statements made by the minister when he gave his annual explanation as to the operation of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. The reasons he assigned for embarking upon this national policy of shipbuilding, as set forth at page 1329 of Hansard, were briefly as follows: First, that the construction of ships for the Canadian Government Mercantile Marine was a war measure. Previous to that time the construction of ships in Canada had been carried on by the Imperial Munitions Board, but the minister expressed the view that it was necessary 
for ships owned by the Canadian people to be built and registered in Canada. I will not comment on that reason at any length -it must stand for what it is worth. The second reason advanced for the shipbuilding programme was that it was intended to assist our railways.
How much ground there is for that statement we may discover when we recall that the predecessors of the present ministry laid their blighting hands upon the one great railway that was intended to carry the products of the West to our Atlantic ports-products that would have yielded freight for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, or any other vessels engaged in the Atlantic trade. When we. learn also that in Halifax harbour there are fourteen of the Government-owned ships swinging idly at their moorings with nothing to do, we get a further idea as to the truth of this second reason given by the minister. We cannot but come to the conclusion that this second reason put forward by him for building a Canadian merchant marine has not measured up to the expectations that were entertained at the time. The third reason mentioned for the Government shipbuilding programme was the desire to expand our export trade. Now, Sir, we were told that no new contracts had been placed since 1919. That was a year after the armistice had been signed and when it was easy enough for the Government to form a fair idea as to what the next year or two might have in store for shipping. In view of the uncertain prospects they should have cancelled the orders then in hand, as they cancelled the contract with the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, and remunerated the contractors. But what I want to discuss more particularly is the fourth reason for the Government undertaking and continuing this shipbuilding programme. The minister stated that it was in order to give employment to skilled workmen who needed it, and especially to our returned soldiers. The minister's own words in presenting this reason are to be found at page 1330 of Hansard where he is reported as saying:
Now, I explained to the House last year, and I repeat the statement, that the Government's reason for continuing the shipbuilding programme was the serious labour conditions that existed throughout Canada at the time of the signing of the Armistice, and which conditions prevailed through the year 1919. Thousands of skilled and unskilled workmen were out of employment in the Dominion; and, as at that time hundreds of thousands of our brave men were returning from the front, the Government felt that it was its plain duty to carry on ship-

building and to give employment not only to the men then needed in the industry, but to others who were likely to require work, and especially the returned soldiers.
Sir, that was the fourth reason given by the minister for entering upon this policy, and especially for its continuance. Let us turn to the closing part of the minister's statement and see if his explanation in that regard was well founded. The remarks in question, as recorded in Hansard, were:
As I stated a moment ago the war was at its height. Material was high and unskilled as well as skilled labour was hard to obtain.
Therefore the experience the Government had in carrying on this work has shown that the main reason advanced for continuing the shipbuilding programme was not well founded, and when they came to employ workmen in the shipyards they found that the skilled and the unskilled labour needed was not available. In the same statement from which I have quoted it is said that the men engaged in the operation of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine as officers, engineers, ordinary seamen, firemen, stewards, et cetra, number 1,674, of whom 868 are Canadians and the balance not of Canadian nationality. It does seem strange to find that only one-half of the men on these vessels are Canadians, when the Government's primary object in going on with their shipbuilding programme was to give work to Canadians and especially returned soldiers. Under the circumstances we are justified in asking the minister to state how many returned soldiers were provided with work in the Canadian shipbuilding yards during the construction of these ships at such great expense to the Canadian exchequer. We are certainly entitled to know why the public money of Canada has not been paid out to those for whom it was intended. That is a piece of information that should have been given to the committee.
In reply to the statement made by the Prime Minister when introducing his motion withdrawing the item from further consideration "modestly sugesting" that the Opposition did not themselves know why the session was continued all night, I would say to him that it was because of our quest for information. It was very evident that when we were pressing for information the Government were anxious to turn that pressure to their own account by calling it obstruction with a view to imposing the closure, and thereby preventing further light from being shed on the shipbuilding programme.
132i
When he presented his annual statement of the operations of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine the minister was asked by some members on this side of the House, and especially by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), to explain why the difference of $148,000 between the amount represented for depreciation in the operating account for 1920 and in the consolidated balance sheet as of December 31, 1920-he figures being $667,000 as against $815,000-did not appear in the operating account of 1919. The minister passed it off by asking the House to accept the statement of certain auditors, namely, Marwick, Mitchell & Company. He was also asked if the item of $22,000 represented the total outstanding liabilities at that date as shown in the operating account for 1920. It has been stated in this committee that liabilities are outstanding against the Canadian Government Merchant Marine in the city of Halifax alone to the amount of $100,000, and mariners from Other ports have represented that liabilities are still outstanding against the merchant marine in the ports where they have been doing business. In view of those statements I think it is only fair that a full explanation should be given by the minister.
With regard to the auditing of the accounts, we have an independent system of auditing in the Auditor General's Department. That is the only department to which this committee can look for accurate information, and when a financial statement such as this under review is questioned by hon. members it is not satisfactory for them to be referred to a firm of auditors who are unknown to the committee in a public way. Further than that, even in our own independent audit through the Auditor General's Department we retain the right at all times to go into any items upon which further information is required and to call for producton of all papers connected therewith. Up to the present time we have not had an opportunity to go into the operating or any other accounts of the Government merchant marine. I think in all justice, Sir, we are entitled to have those accounts referred to that committee, especially in view of the fact that they have been challenged-I do not think the word is too strong-by members of the committee.
Another matter that has not been properly explained in the minister's statement is the interest account. It has been shown by some hon. members that the interest on the cost of construction for 1919,

amounting to $1,300,000, has been discharged to the extent of $500,000 only; the interest for 1920, amounting to $2,700,000, is still due to the Receiver General, and there is also interest outstanding on advances on account of progress payments for 1920.
In view of the fact that all requests for the information I have indicated have been dismissed by the minister referring hon. members to a firm of outside auditors, I think the committee was quite justified in pressing for that information, and I am at a loss to understand how the Minister of Marine or any other hon. gentleman can say that obstructive tactics were employed warranting the imposition of the closure. It does appear to me that the Government were simply looking for some excuse to apply the closure in order to escape giving the information asked for. In order to put the matter in concrete form so that the minister may give a full explanation, if he sees fit, I propose to put a series of questions which the minister may take an opportunity to answer during the course of this debate. These are the questions:
1.	Why was the difference in depreciation between the amount mentioned in the operating account for 1920 and the amount mentioned in the consolidated balance sheet as of December 31, 1920, of $148,000, not accounted for in the balance sheet of 1919 or in the operating account of 1920?
2.	What explanation is given by the management as to the outstanding liabilities known to exist at Halifax * of about $100,000 and at other ports where the boats of the merchant marine have entered and cleared.
3.	Why has the Canadian Government Merchant Marine not paid the full amount of interest due to the Canadian treasury, namely, the interest on progress payments on cost of construction advanced in 1918, the balance of interest due in 1919 of $800,000 out of a total of $1,300,000, the amount of interest due for 1920 on cost of construction of about $2,700,000, and the amount of interest due on advances on progress payments for 1920?
4.	How many keels were laid at the end of 1919, the date when the minister said the contracts were all let?
5.	How many of the 868 Canadians employed on Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships are returned soldiers?
6.	Why are almost one-half of the men employed on Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships of other nationalities

than Canadian when one of the main reasons given for carrying through this programme was to give work to Canadian workmen?
7.	How many returned soldiers were given work in Canadian yards?
I think, Sir, the committee is justly entitled to a full and explicit explanation of these matters before the minister can honestly charge the committee with obstruction and in order to fully justify the carrying out of these contracts.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: What is the date?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
It was assented to on June 6, 1919. This is the preamble:
Whereas notwithstanding the armistice of the eleventh day of November last, and the extension thereof which has been granted by His Majesty and His Allies, has suspended the actual operations of the war between His Majesty and the German Emperior, the Emperor of Austria, King of Hungary, the Sultan of Turkey, and the King of the Bulgarians, it is necessary that measures should continue to be taken for the common defence and security : and whereas it is also necessary to provide for the demobilization of the Canadian forces; and to this end it is expedient that aid as hereinafter provided be rendered to His Majesty: Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows :
Then clause 2 reads that payment of $350,000,000 may be made, for what purposes?
(a)	the defence and security of Canada;
(b)	the conduct of naval and military operations in or beyond Canada and the demobilization of the Canadian forces;
(c)	the promoting of trade and industry, and transportation facilities therefor;
(d)	the carrying out of any measures deemed necessary or advisable by the Governor-inCouncil in consequence of the war; and
(e)	payments made or expenditure incurred during the fisoal year ending the 31st day of March, 1919, for the purposes mentioned in The War Appropriation Act, 1918, and in excess of the amount authorized by the said Act.
So that, all of a sudden, towards the end of the session in 1918, the acting Prime Minister came with a resolution asking Parliament to vote a lump sum of $350,000,000 for war purposes, as alleged in the preamble, and if the minister will refer to Hansard, he will see that on May 7, 1910, it reads:
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
War expenditures, $350,000,000.
And it is out of that vote that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries asked permission to take the appropriation of $30,000,000 odd.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
Yes. It is out of that appropriation that my hon. friend took his $30,000,000. We debated the resolution. I was one of the first to speak on it. I objected to the military expenditure, hut

I was answered by the then Minister of Militia and Defence, the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn), who explained that the money was needed for military purposes. Then we discussed the question of naval expenditure, and my hon. friend gave his explanations. Finally we came to the clause dealing with transportation. That was the shipbuilding programme, and that is where I said that I was in favour of a wise and moderate expenditure for that purpose. I shall read what I said on that occasion. My hon. friend read only part of my speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
Would the hon.
member kindly give us the date?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: May 7 and 8, 1919.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: If my hon. friend will turn over a few pages, he will find there was a $30,000,000 vote put under the Marine Department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
Possibly, but it was taken out of this vote:
War expenditures, $350,000,000 vote.
Under that vote my hon. friend spoke, and my deskmate, the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) also spoke, and then I said:
I am a Canadian, first, last and always, and I sincerely approve of the policy of any government which will promote our shipbuilding and improve our transportation facilities.
A little later on I said:
I stand for a moderate and wise policy of shipbuilding for Canada, and If the Acting Prime Minister, under section 2 of the Bill, intends to apply some of that money for the promotion of shipbuilding and the improvement and development of our Canadian transportation facilities, I shall vote for the amount which is being asked this evening.
But I qualified that statement by adding that the money should be spent wisely and moderately. My hon. friend, however, went headlong and gave contracts to all the shipyards of Canada. My hon. friend persists in saying "You have approved that policy." I said that I would approve a wise and moderate expenditure. My hon. friend, the moment he saw, as was stated by the president of the Bank of Montreal in his address at the annual meeting of the shareholders, a shrinkage in the cost of tonnage as between the prices of 1919 and those of today, should have stopped. Did he not cancel the contract with the Dominion Steel Company when he found out that the prices were exorbitant? My hon. friend said: "I

was approved by the hon. member for Mai-sonnuve." I qualified that approval. Let me go further. Supposing I had fully approved that vast expenditure of money, am I my hon. friend's guardian? Have I anything to do with the Government? My hon. friend had my approval, but it was a qualified approval, and when the hon. gentleman saw the shrinkage in prices, it was his duty, as a minister and an administrator of the King's purse, to stop that wanton expenditure. I say that I criticized that resolution; I warned the Prime Minister at the time. I said:
I am afraid that my hon. friend has become colour blind in money matters. A dollar, a hundred dollars, a thousand dollars-there is no difference between them to my hon. friend. He has been rolling in millions and billions since the beginning of the war, and I am afraid he ha.s lost his sense of proportion. Whether he speaks of one million or one billion, it is all the same to him. Perhaps it is due to the fact that he is an optimist; but there are limits to optimism. My hon. friend should not forget that Canada has a population of barely eight million, that we have a war debt of two billion dollars, and that although the resources of the country are immense, it may not be an easy thing in this general bankruptcy of the world to develop our resources. To develop our resources we shall need the aid of foreign capital, and in order to obtain the aid of foreign capital we must certainly maintain our credit on the safety line, but I am afraid my hon. friend has long since left the safety line.
These are the words of warning which I gave to the hon. gentleman and to the Acting Prime Minister. I criticized conscientiously, I think, the large sum which Parliament was asked to vote on that occasion and under which my hon. friend found shelter to spend the $30,000,000 for the shipbuilding venture.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I do not like to interrupt the hon. member, but I must remind him that he has only one minute more.	-

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I do not intend to go beyond the time fixed by the rules; but I repeat to my hon. friend that it was as easy for him as representing the Crown to cancel any of those contracts as he at first cancelled the contracts with the Dominion Steel Company when he realized that the prices asked for steel plates would, if adhered to, be a scandal in the administration of his department.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
Alternating between the two sides of the chamber, I should give the floor to Mr. Ballantyne. I must remind him, however, that if he replies immediately to the hon. member for Maisonneuve he

will have exhausted his right to speak, and will be precluded from replying to any other member.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I first of all must thank my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) for withdrawing, partially at least, what he somewhat hastily said the other day about my losing my business reputation in the city of Montreal. My hon. friend said, if I understood him correctly, that when I introduced this shipbuilding policy on April 4, 1918, I stated at that time that it was for war purposes alone.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
No. The other day,
when I was critising my hon. friend, I said that I had voted for a moderate and wise expenditure, because although the armistice had been signed we were still at war, and it was a war vote. My hon. friend denied that, and pointed out that the armistice had been signed in November, and that the resolution was introduced in the month of May by the Acting Prime Minister. I point out again that the preamble shows that it was a war expenditure, that the appropriation was for war purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
My hon. friend is getting somewhat mixed in his statement. I am referring to the first day when I mentioned the Government shipbuilding programme in this House on April 4, 1918.
I then stated that these ships, in addition to being required for war purposes, would also be required for other purposes. I shall quote only a sentence or two of my statement at that time. I said:
We require ships for our coal trade, we require ships to carry the products of the farm, and we shall require ships to work in conjunction with the Government-owned transcontinental railways.
I quote that just to show that I have been perfectly consistent all the way through. While I said that the war was the paramount reason for the Government adopting this shipbuilding policy, which as hon. gentlemen know received the unanimous approval of the House at that time, I also made it very clear to the House that the Government Merchant Marine would be required to carry the products not only of the farm but of our industries in helping to expand our export trade, and to work in conjunction with the transcontinental railway system, which was Government-owned at that time.
To come back to the remarks made by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve on May 8, 1919, which I quoted in this House the
other day, it is quite true as he says that he made those remarks on a war appropriation vote intoduced by the Acting Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Sir Thomas White, but if my hon. friend will turn back a few pages, to page 2202 of Hansard of May 8, 1919, he will see that there was then under a discussion a vote under the Marine Department of $30,000,000 to continue the Government shipbuilding programme. I have read very carefully the debate on that $30,000,000 vote several times, and I have failed to find one word from the lips of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve opposing this further vote of $30,000,000. The war was over then. This was on May 8, 1919, and the armistice had been signed on November 11, 1918. If my hon. friend held the same yiews then that he holds now, then was the time and this was the place for him to have risen and said: The armistice has been signed and the war is over; I favoured a shipbuilding policy for war only; I cannot give my support to this $30,000,000 vote that the Government is now asking. But he did nothing of the sort. He will not find one word of his in that whole debate in opposition to that $30,000,000 vote. I think my hon. friend was perfectly right in his attitude at that time, and I think he is wrong now in making such a quick rightabout turn. The war appropriation vote that my hon. friend has referred to tonight had nothing whatever to do with the $30,000,000 vote. This $30,000,000 vote was not a war appropriation vote but an estimate of the Marine Department. When the war appropriation vote was up my hon. friend asked the Prime Minister if any portion of that vote would be used for shipbuilding, to which the acting Prime Minister replied " yes " and my hon. friend went on to make his speech, but what 1 want to make abundantly clear now as I did the other day was that when this $30,000,000 vote in the Marine Estimates was under discussion, if my hon. friend held the views then that he holds now, he should have opposed that $30,000,000 vote but he did not do so. No matter how my hon. friend may have argued a moment ago the Hansard is there to prove my statement that I have had the support of my hon. friend on the shipbuilding policy right up to the present session. My hon. friend thinks that he now senses public opinion against public ownership. I do not want to take up the time of this committee like hon. friends opposite have done by reading reports from newspapers from one end

of the country to the other but wherever hon. gentlemen opposite have read an editorial against the Government policy I could have read a dozen in favour of it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Why did you not do it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I would not waste so much time. I am very glad that hon. gentlemen do oppose the Government shipbuilding programme, because as a rule my hon. friends opposite are to be found on the wrong side of public opinion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: You will see at the next election.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: And I thank them for their opposition to one of the most popular policies that has ever been introduced and put into effect by a government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: The minister is at sea.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: My hon. friend talked for hours and hours the other night and I think he ought to allow me to continue my remarks without further interruption.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Provided the minister addresses the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Maisonneuve has referred to some financial men in the city of Montreal, he knows and I know that the business men in Montreal are opposed to public ownership; they have been so for years and are so now, so it is not to wondered at that the president of the Bank of Montreal or the president of any other bank should voice an opinion against public ownership. Hon. gentlemen opposite, especially my hon friend from St. James, Montreal, take a great deal of delight in quoting the Montreal Gazette, but I notice that my hon. friend never quoted any of the great French Papers of Montreal. La Presse of Montreal with a daily circulation of 140,000 has had nothing but commendation of the Government shipbuilding programme. The same is true of La Patrie. When my hon. friends get an opportunity to go before the constituencies they represent in this House, especially my friends from the province of Quebec and the Maritime Provinces, they will find a very strong public opinion in favour of the Government mercantile marine. Make no mistake about that. As I said a moment ago, hon. gentlemen opposite generally get on the wrong side of these public questions, and therefore I do not very much mind the strenuous opposition they have offered to this vote. Now, there are some ludicrous sides to public 
life. My hon. friends the other night deliberately planned to obstruct the passage of this item.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Well, we have the right on this side to entertain our own opinion on that point. The member for Queen's (Mr. Sinclair) sat silently with his brave colleagues on the other side the other-evening from half-past nine o'clock, right on until the following afternoon at four o'clock, and yet he says now that the minister gave him no opportunity to express his opinion on the Government's shipbuilding programme. He therefore has to rise tonight in his place and register his opposition to it. I am amazed at the conduct of hon. gentlemen. They were so hard put to it to keep the debate going that my young friend from Charlevoix (Mr. Casgrain), the member for St. James division (Mr. Rinfret), and the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), had to make a dozen speeches; and as the night wore on and the grey dawn came, I could see these young men giving out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Well, you looked like it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
We are good for
another night if you want it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: These gentlemen, I am sure, would have welcomed the member for Queen's had he entered the debate which they started. Now, Mr. Chairman, I rose principally to state that the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) gave the Government and me his full support, by voice and vote, in connection with the $30,000,000 on May 8 last, and nothing in the pages of Hansard will appear to the contrary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: The programme was completed twice that year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Frontenac and the Prime Minister the other day endeavoured to hold me to what they considered my share of responsibility for this whole vote passed on this occasion, May 8,	1919. That vote, as
the minister has pointed out, was
for $30,000,000. I should be glad if the minister would give me his attention. When Parliament voted that money it was not an instruction to the minister to go on with shipbuilding; it was only an authorization for him to spend money upon ships; and if the minister had exercised that good business judgment which I believe he has always displayed in his private business, he would have recognized the fact that everywhere in the world ships were being built and only one result could ensue, namely, an increase in shipping, whicih would mean a decline in rates as well as a decrease in the cost of producing ships. The minister knows that today the world has almost 20,000,000 tons more shipping than in 1914. Did he cease letting contracts? No, he did not. And here, let me remind the committee once more that this was after I had left the Government. After July 1, 1919, contracts were let for 20 ships by my hon. friend the minister.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: By tender?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Will you allow me a question?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Gertainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
My hon. friend
was a member of the Government when it was decided to continue the shipbuilding programme for reasons that I have already given. My hon. friend was a member of the Government when the thirty millions were voted. The other ten millions my hon. friend talks about was in addition to those thirty millions and constituted a balance from the previous year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
The Minister of Marine stated on July 5, that the supplementary vote he was then asking for was to complete the shipbuilding programme. Now does he mean to say that when he came back the following year and asked for twenty millions, as he did on March 23, 1920, and when he comes to-day and asks for this vote of eight millions as he is doing, that this is in accordance with his statement of July 5, 1919? It requires a very far stretch of the imagination to see it. But let us come back to this matter of building ships. I want the committee to understand this fact. My hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) made his statement the other day in good faith-I am quite certain of that-and I do not for a moment wish to attribute any bad-faith

to my right hon. friend the leader of the Government. He made the statement that I was in the Government when every contract was let. He later corrected that statement as far as two ships were concerned. But I point out to the committee, and I take my information from the report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries for the year 1919-20, that after July 1, r_ 1919, contracts were let for twenty ships and of these, contracts for ten ships were let in 1920.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Where does my hon. friend get his information?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I take the information from the report submitted by the Department of Marine and Fisheries which I hold in my hand. I could even give the names of the ships, but I do not wish to do that because it would take too much time. Any member can find the information on page 15 of the report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1920.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
May I ask my hon.
friend one question?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I have only twenty minutes at my disposal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I will only occupy a second and it is in order to get information. Can my hon. friend tell me how many contracts were let after March 31, 1920?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
There were two contracts let after March 31, 1920. Accord-[DOT] ing to this information these contracts were let on April 7 of that year, for ships to be built in Vancouver. Now I think that pretty effectively disposes of my hon. friend's contention. I recognize this fact -that in the changing conditions taking place after the termination of the war a decline in values was bound to occur, but I think fhe Minister of Marine and Fisheries is open to criticism in this respect, that he did not foresee the decline in the value of ships that was taking place. They saw it in the United States, and I want to tell the committee that many of the United States shipyards were dismantled long before my hon. friend quit letting contracts in Canada. To-day what are the circumstances? We have sixteen ships, according to the information given to the committee the other night, under construction in shipyards in Canada. I am told that two ships were recently put upon the stocks in the
TMr. Crerar.l
city of Halifax, and those ships are costing the country $191.50 a ton on an average. We are building ships to-day, as a result of this improvident policy. When they are completed we can* turn round and write off fifty per cent of the cost and then they will be overvalued. That is anything but a sound business proposal bearing in mind the financial conditions this country is in.
Now I want to offer a word of criticism
and I wish to do it in a most friendly manner because I am sure the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows that I have no personal animus towards him-of the balance sheet submitted by the minister the other day. If we have a bad situation in regard to our ships let us face it frankly. I know that is what my hon. friend does in his private business, and that is what every other hon. member has to do in similar circumstances. The depreciation allowed on these ships is apparently just about sufficient to write them off in fifty years as nearly as I can figure it. If I am wrong I want to be corrected.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I am sorry the hon. member was not here during the allnight sitting as the hon. member for Red Deer was. He then would have heard my explanation in that regard. However I have no objection to explain it again.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I will read your explanation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: The debate must close at two o'clock and the minister should seek the permission of all the members of the House if he wishes to speak.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
The
hon. member for Marquette asked a question and I understand the minister is willing to answer it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: He has exhausted his right to speak.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
At any rate I think I am quite correct in this statement that if the shipping company had been charged interest on the value of the ships turned over to it at the rate of the Government are paying on the Victory loans the people of Canada subscribed for, the deficit on the operations of these ships would not be short of $1,000,000 for the past year. That is not a sound business position, and I think it is as well for us to place the facts frankly before the people. They should be

told just what these ships are doing financially and whether they are operated on a business basis. The minister talks about the splendid financial position the venture is in. He says that no bank loans are shown in the balance sheet and the operating company is in an easy position financially. No wonder it is in an easy position financially. When this country is putting up all the money for the building of these vessels it may well be. But I would suggest to my hon. friend-and this is the last word I have to say-that if he is in a position to bring in another annual statement to this House-which is a very problematical thing-I hope that it will give the position of this shipping concern in a plain business way such as any ordinary business concern would do in presenting a statement to its shareholders.
Upon Mr. Stevens and Mr. Sinclair rising together:

I neecj scarcely tell the committee that I am opposed to the shipbuilding policy of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I never approved of that policy from its inception, and I took occasion several times to tell my hon. friend what my views were in regard to this matter. On Monday night I spent the evening with him. We talked the matter over and we were very frank with one another in exchanging our views. I said that as a business proposition his policy was a mistake and he was not able to convince me to the contrary. The minister has taunted us with reading newspaper extracts. There were some newspaper extracts used, but I have no recollection of quoting any
myself. But when my hon. friend refers to newspapers, I want to draw to his attention the fact that there is a prominent newspaper in the city of Ottawa, called the Ottawa Journal, that has condemned his policy. I also want to tell him that there is a prominent paper supporting the party to which he now belongs, published in his own city, the Montreal Gazette, that day by day has condemned his policy; and I know no more sound financial paper in the Dominion. We have in the province of Nova Scotia a leading Conservative paper that has supported the Conservative party for the last forty-five, years or more, that faithfully supported the Union party, and that now supports the present party in power, but there is nothing that paper can say too strong in condemnation of the policy of my hon. friend. These facts we brought to his attention the other night, and I was surprised to-night to learn that the only newspaper that he was able to quote in his favour from Cape Breton to Vancouver was La Patrie of Montreal. I do not have the pleasure of reading that newspaper and therefore do not know much about its views, but if it is true as my hon. friend contends that the press is with him he should have been able to cite other newspapers besides La Patrie.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: What about the Globe?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING

The
hon. member for Guysborough has the floor.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: In my judgment, Mr. Chairman, the little group of men who stood to their guns on Monday night and presented this item from passing did a national service. They focussed attention on this question, and the newspapers from one end of the country to the other have given it a good deal of notice since that time. I want to say also that the official Opposition got very effective help on that occasion from my hon. friends from Red Deed (Mr. Clark) and Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg). Now the people know the facts, to some extent at least, and if after knowing all the details they want to have another white elephant on their hands like that which the Minister of Railways has presented to them-

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
We have not got any.
Mr. SINCLAIR (Guysborough),: I say if they want to have another white elephant like that which the Minister of Railways now has on his hands, that is their own affair and they will have themselves to blame for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: You gave us a white elephant.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING

My
hon. friend says that we gave him a white elephant.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Yes, the Grand Trunk Pacific.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Order, order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I want to tell him that he was very willing to take it. Besides that is only a baby elephant compared with the Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk. I have watched my hon. friend's career as Minister of Railways, I know his responsibility in regard to those matters and if I had the time to tell him all about it, it would put him in a serious light before the country. We all know my hon. friend is to a very large extent responsible for the railway situation. He is responsible for the Canadian Northern deal, which he put through this House by closure. He is responsible for the Grand Trunk deal, which he also forced through this House against the best that we could do in opposition to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: That was a good bargain.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING

But
when the Grand Trunk deal was put through the House, if I recollect rightly, my hon. friend told us that it was going to be a paying proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING

We

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Mr. Chairman

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Sit down.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: A point of order is always in order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Simcoe rises to a point of order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: My point of order is that the hon. member is not speaking to the motion; he is discusing railways, not shipping.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I am sure that on being reminded that he is departing slightly from the question the hon. member will return to it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
I was interrupted by the Minister of Railways, hence the digression. In my remarks I made the mistake of calling this movement a policy. I submit that it is not a policy. If my hon. friend the Minister of Marine had devised some policy by which the people of Canada could become a shipbuilding and ship-owning nation, then he would have done an important service foi the country. But that is not the kind o: policy that he has launched. Why, Mr Chairman, anyone could do what the hon. gentleman has done. He has built ships at profiteering prices. That is all. It does not take very much statesmanship to do that. The chief messenger of the House of Commons, if you gave him $2,000,000 and sent him out on the streets of any city on this continent or on the continent of Europe could purchase a ship as good as the 10,000-ton ships that my hon. friend has built, pay the market price and have a balance over sufficient to make himself comfortable for the rest of his life. So this is really not a policy at all; it is spending the people's money by giving contracts to build ships at profiteering prices.
But there is one point to which I particularly wish to refer, and it is my principal reason for getting on my feet tonight. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister, in his speech last evening, attempted to fasten on the Opposition responsibility for the position we are now in in regard to this shipping policy. Here is what my right hon. friend said:
That policy was embarked upon, if I am correctly informed, with the unanimous approval of this House in the first place. That was in the spring of the year 1918.
You will notice his language: the policy was embarked upon with the approval of the House of Commons. I wish to be permitted to contradict that statement. The

Minister of Marine announced this policy in Montreal on January 4, 1918. Referring to a statement which I find in that well-known publication by Castell Hopkins, The Canadian National Review, p. 440, I find the following:
Mr. Ballantyne's Shipbuilding Projects. As Minister of Marine and Fisheries and Naval Service, the Hon. C. C. Ballantyne devoted much attention to the promotion of shipbuilding as a war-time necessity for transportation and a great impetus to Canadian industry and after war prosperity. On January 4, 1918-
You will note the date, Mr. Chairman.
-he announced an elaborate Government policy in this conection which would implement pre-election pledges.
I would like to know to whom the preelection pledges were given in the election of 1917. Were they given to those parties who subsequently got the contracts?
Under it the Government proposed to utilize, to their utmost capacity of about 300,000 tons annually, all existing Canadian shipyards for the production of modern steel cargo steamers.
The point I would like to make is that on January 4, 1918, the minister announced his policy in Montreal. This policy was therefore not inaugurated with the consent of Parliament. It was started behind closed doors in the usual way in which this Government have carried on all their policies 

by Order in Council. Proceedings were taken under that Order in Council prior to the date when Parliament heard of the shipbuilding policy, and we are told by the Review I have quoted that the policy was announced to implement pre-election pledges. The fact is-and I want the Prime Minister to note it-that he entered into this shipbuilding policy months before Parliament knew anything about it. He did not wait for the approval of Parliament; he launched the policy under Order in Council and it was announced by his minister on January 4, 1918, three months before it was reported to Parliament. Contracts were let and ships were in course of construction when Parliament first heard of it. This was admitted by the minister when he made his first statement on April 4, 1918, when the minister made his announcement in the House of Commons. He used this language:
At the present time we are having two ships built by the Vickers Company of Montreal-
"At the present time"; that is April 4, 1918.
-we are having two ships built by the Vickers Company of Montreal, one of 8,100 tons dead weight capacity, an 11-knot ship, and another of 4,350 tons.
In addition to the two ships that are being built by the Canadian Vickers Company for the Canadian Government, another ship of about five thousand tons is being built by the Wallace Shipbuilding Company at Vancouver. Another vessel of 3,550 tons is being built by the Collingwood Shipbuilding Company, of Collingwood.
This statement appears in Hansard of 1918, volume 1, page 346. It appears, therefore, that three months before the policy was announced in the House of Commons it had been adopted by the Government by Order in Council, money had been spent, keels had been laid, ships were in course of construction." Is it fair under these circumstances for the Prime Minister to say that the policy was inaugurated with the consent of both sides of this House? I say, Sir, it was inaugurated without the consent of anybody in the House of Commons; so far as it appears, the Prime Minister did noit even consult his own party. The responsibility for this shipping programme rest altogether upon the Government. This baby must be placed on their doorstep along with the number of others of the same type.
It has been admitted by my hon. friend, admitted by everybody, that this shipbuilding programme is a losing business, I pointed that out to my hon, friend in 1919, but he would not listen. I tried to persuade him to drop it but he hardened his heart. The calculation I made at that time was a very simple one, and in order to remind the Minister of it I will repeat it here;
I took as an illustration one of the 10,000 ton ships that he has built in the shipyards at Halifax. These ships cost approximately $200 a ton; therefore the total cost of one ship would be $2,000,000. I want to compare the fixed charges on that ship with those on a ship built on the Clyde or in any of the yards in Europe and Britain prior to the war. There are millions of tons of shipping on the sea now which were built prior to the war and which cost only $50 a ton. I make that comparison not for the purpose of showing that ships could be built for $50 a ton at the present time, but to emphasize how impossible it is for my hon. friend to make any money, with the present rates of freight, in competition with ships built at $50 a ton. Now, take the fixed charges: insurance at 3 per cent would be $60,000. I submit that careful business men approve of 5 per cent depreciation on the capital invested. A steel steamer is a very perishable piece of property; the machinery has to be renewed, the hull will rust and boilers have to be re-

newed every ten years. An average life of a steamer is supposed to be about twenty years and then you must have money enough to replace her, if you are to remain in the business. The insurance at 3 per cent would be $60,000; the depreciation at 5 per cent would amount to $100,000. The interest on the money invested on the construction of these ships would be figured at the rate of 5 1-2 per cent, or $110,000. The total fixed charges, therefore, would be $270,000. In other words, the steamer would have to earn $270,000 before she could begin to make a profit for her owners. Now, take the fixed charges on a steamer of the same size, and the same earning capacity as the 10,000 ton ship, costing $50 a ton. The total cost would be $500,000; insurance at 3 per cent $15,000; depreciation at 5 per cent, $25,000; interest at 6 per cent-for I suppose a private owner would have to pay 6 per cent-$30,000; total fixed charges on that ship $70,000. The fixed charge on the ship built at Halifax is $270,000; subtracting one from the other you have a handicap of $200,000 as against my hon. friend's ship. How then does my hon. friend expect under these circumstances to compete and pay his way with vessels built at one quarter the cost. That is to say, a ship built by my hon. friend in Halifax will have to earn each year $200,000 more than the other one in order to keep out of insolvency.
That is not, however, the whole story. Those hon. gentlemen who were here a few evenings ago when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) was getting his Estimates through will remember that we passed subsidies for certain lines, and amongst those lines I want to give the committee three that are competitors with the lines on which the Government propose to put their ships.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has one minute more.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
My time should not be exhausted by these interruptions. One of these routes was to Australia. As regards the route to Australia, my hon. friend is paying his competitors $130,000 of a subsidy so that the Government ships-will start with that handicap. Another one was to hte West Indies. We voted $340,000 for a service to the West Indies. According to the Minister of Marine three Government ships are to be put on this route. The same is true of the line to Newfoundland. I say it is bad business to put Government ships
[Mr. Sinclair.)
on a certain route and then for the Government to pay its competitor a sum of money to enable the competitor to drive the Government ships out of the business.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-[DOT][DOT]

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: M. l'Orateur-

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Mr. Chairman

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: M. l'Orateur-

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
I'desire to say a few
words in reply to the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), as well as a few words in reply to the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). The minister, of course, is not permitted to make further statements-

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Your time is up.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr Stevens) has the floor.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
Four or five hon.
members stood up. I should like to know who will be recognized next.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I might point out just at this moment that the hon. member, having spoken, has exhausted his right to speak. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre has the floor.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
I was saying, Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member for Marquette who, I am sorry, is not in his seat, that he was seeking to justify his action when he was a member of the Government. I wish to point this out to the committee, for the purpose of clearing up what was apparently a misunderstanding in the mind of the hon. member for Marquette, that the contracts for the ships were arranged for and awarded during 1919. Some of the terms of the contract, it is true, were under discussion and were not finally settled until the early months of 1920; but as regards the awarding of the contract, the last one was awarded in December, 1919. But this does not change the important feature which was pointed out by the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne), and that is this, that when the policy was launched, when this House undertook the expenditure of, first, $30,000,000 and later other expenditures, the leader of the Agrarian party, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) was a

member, a consenting member of the Government to this matter, and, furthermore, he supported it in the House. My hon. friend made another point-and it was also referred to by the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough-that the depreciation is not properly taken care of by the method of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and his staff. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries pointed out the other day that he set aside, as a fund for depreciation, two per cent. That has been brought into question; it is quite right that it should be, and I am going to make an explanation which, I think, will meet the question raised by the hon. member (Mr. Sinclair) as well as the hon. member for Marquette. Two per cent set aside and invested at 5i per cent interest compounded for twenty-five years represents the whole cost of these vessels. In other words, the department secured from an actuary a careful figuring of what was necessary to set aside for a fund which would fully cover the cost of the ships over a period of twenty-five years. That, I say, is a sound, safe and businesslike policy.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
Can
the hon. member give us those figures?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I can; I happen to have them under my hand. I have not the exact figures but the hon. member can figure them out readily. Two per cent amounts to about $20,000 a year, and at 51 per cent compound interest for twenty-five years, he will find that it comes to the value of the ships. That is a sound businesslike proposition. My hon. friend suggested five per cent. Five per cent treated in the same way would far more than cover the need.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: These ships were built on borrowed money at 51 per cent. What about the interest?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
I am glad my hon.
friend raised the question, because it reminds me of something that was overlooked during the discussion the other day. In 1919, out of operating profits, the minister paid $500,000 of interest into the Consolidated Fund, which was the complete interest charge for the ships in commission at that time. It is true that this year the department was not able to do the same thing to the same extent, but last year interest was paid. I admit what my hon. friend is driving at, that in case the operating expenses do not provide for the
full interest charges, that would be an accumulating amount and there is no question of that. I want however to make this point quite clear, that two per cent set aside makes absolute provision for replacement of the ships in twenty-five years' time.
My hon. friend raised another point as regards installation of boilers every ten years. That is a question of repairs. After the first or second year, there will be annual repairs to these ships; engines will have to be repaired in part; plates will be bent or worn out or rusted, and they will have to be replaced. All that, however, will be charged up against operating expenses. That is a part of the ordinary repairs from day to day and from year to year and does not enter into depreciation at all. The depreciation fund is provided in the way I have stated. It has been suggested repeatedly in this debate that a full depreciation, figured on a basis of the cheapest possible ship to secure in the world as compared with the cost of these ships, should be written off this year. That is the most absurd suggestion from a business standpoint that I have heard. Take, for instance, any man's business, whether it is in goods or in a plant, machinery or anything else. Simply because the market has temporarily collapsed and fallen, he does not during that period, or in that year, or in that accounting period, write off the full amont of the supposed or alleged loss. No business man will do that. If he makes a fair provision for depreciation, he is doing all that can reasonably be asked. I draw attention to the exact figures set aside for depreciation this year, $667,665.46. That is the amount, and I contend it is sound business. Does my hon. friend or any other hon. gentleman, who has been vigorously attacking the minister in the last few days, suggest that trading conditions of the world are going to remain in their present, abnormal unforeseen and unexpected condition for the full period of twenty-five years, or even for	ten or five	years?
Nobody thinks that for a moment. I think all hon. gentlemen will agree with me in this, that this condition was utterly unexpected. It is true that some business men foresaw that a time would come of what is known as reconstruction, a time when business would have to be re-adjusted, but I suggest to my hon. friend who has just taken his seat this: that when the hon. member for Marquette, the hon. member for Lunenburg, and others attack the Min-

ister of Marine in terms something ike this-you should have foreseen this business collapse and not entered upon this policy-they are condemning in those very terms their own lack of wisdom, because not one of these hon. gentlemen foresaw it himself.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: We told him to sell the ships last year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
Year after year they have supported the Government programme. It is true that last year there was some mild opposition; it was not very vigorous.
Let me say a word or two to my hon. friend who has offered, I will not say harsh, for he never is harsh, but some criptic criticism at all events. He said a moment ago that this policy was introduced by the back-door route. Now that is not'a fair statement, with all due deference to my hon. friend's usual fairness. What were the conditions? Simply these. In 1918 the world was appalled at the loss of tonnage, literally appalled; this House was appalled; and when the Minister of Marine in the fall of 1917 or the early winter of 1918 decided on his policy and announced it in January in Montreal, what did he do? He did not wait, it is true, until the House met before he arranged to give contracts, because you cannot start the construction of a large ship in a day or so; it takes a couple of months at least to gelt the thing under way. What did the minister do? Knowing the need, he took time by the forelock and let one contract before the House met, and for that he has been criticised. I say that if he had not done so, he would have been criticised at that very session.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I was criticising the minister for saying that this measure was introduced with the approval of both sides of Parliament. My point was that it was not, but that it was introduced by Order in Council three months before Parliament knew anything about it. I was not talking about the necessity on account of the war.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
I am talking about the necessity on account of the war and pointing out why the minister took the action he did. I have this to say to my hon. friend. The Minister of Marine came to this House early in 1918 and announced what he had done. He laid on the table his Estimates, and sat in this House and reviewed those Estimates day after day with

my hon. friend sitting opposite. He did that in 1918; he did that in 1919; he did that again in the fall of 1919; he did it last year, 1920; and here we come to 1921, the fifth session, and this is the first word of criticism of the introduction of this policy.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I opposed it in 1919 and 1920.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
My hon. friend, it is true, made some criticism last year, but I submit that up to within the last half hour not one word of criticism has been offered of the introduction of this policy. My hon. friend has sat silent in his seat for four years and now he comes to-night, five sessions afterwards, and says that the policy was introduced by the back-door route, and hon. gentlemen opposite cheered his statement. What is the inference? If there is any intelligence in the remark, if there is anything in the cheers, they mean simply this, that the minister did something that was wrong. Yet hon. gentlemen sat silent for five sessions, never said a word about it, not one solitary word. I say criticism of that kind is unfair.
Now I come to another point. It has been stated that there is no support of this policy in the press of this country. The Minister of Marine said to-night that he would not take up the time of the committee reading long editorials, but there were placed on Hansard the other day several excerpts from different newspapers in the country, from the Toronto Globe, the Vancouver Province, the Winnipeg Tribune, the Mail and Empire, Toronto; The Sydney Post, and the Hamilton Spectator. I am not going to read them again because they are all on Hansard, but I submit that there are many, many other articles in the leading newspapers of this country approving this policy, as the whole country approved of it when there was, seemingly, prosperity behind the venture-

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Seemingly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Yes, seemingly. It was endorsed and accepted by hon. gentlemen opposite, but when the collapse came, when we were in a difficult position-

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I thought there was a surplus. Does my hon. friend admit that there was a collapse?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I said a business collapse. My hon. friend cannot twist my words in that way. I have used the term repeatedly, that there has been a business collapse.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
Collapsible
boats, he means.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
There has been a complete business collapse throughout the world, particularly in shipping. Now I am going to read an article from the Toronto Globe of Wednesday, April 13, 1920; that is to-day. I notice that my hon. friends opposite have been very anxious to quote from the Montreal Gazette, which I think every one in Canada holds in high regard as a paper of standing, but with very definite views on certain lines, and particularly is it opposed to public ownership. Now I am going to quote from the Toronto Globe, which my hon. friends opposite will agree with me is worthy of consideration in an expression of views on a subject of this kind. On the fourth page of to-day's Toronto Globe, in an editorial under the heading ''Canada's Merchant Marine" I find this:
The Government's Merchant Marine System is vigorously attacked by the Opposition. The reasons for establishing it were explained by Mr. Bailantyne in a recent statement to the House of Commons. First, it was necessary to replace losses in shipping tonnage occasioned by the war. Second, it was advisable to complete the chain of transportation afforded, by the National Transcontinental System of railways. Third, it was desirable to create facilities for the expansion of Canada's export trade. Peace removed the first cause, but the shipbuilding programme was continued for the purpose of furnishing employment to returned soldiers and others. There are now in commission 47 vessels, having an approximate deadweight tonnage of 259,783 tons. The entire programme, when completed, will be 63 vessels with a dead-weight tonnage of 374,284 tons.
Then, after another paragraph, the editorial concludes-

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Read it all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
I will if I have time. The editorial concludes with this:
Canada has on her hands a fleet of ships that must either be sold at a sacrifice or operated in connection with the Canadian National railways to the best possible advantage and with the very highest business ability which can be attracted to the public service. The Globe believes the latter course to be in the public interest.
I have read that for this particular purpose; my hon. friends opposite suggest as the sole solution of this question that the ships should be sold. The other day I pointed out to them the lack of common business sense in attempting to sell these ships at this particular time when, as they themselves say, the shipping market is at the lowest ebb it has reached for many
years. I submit that the point we have been urging right along is a wise one, that these ships should be operated in conjunction with the great Government Railway system for the purpose of developing export trade, and operated as part of the great system of nationally-owned facilities of this great Dominion. That is the policy urged by the minister, and it is the policy that is supported by the Toronto Globe. It is the hope expressed in the various articles to which I have referred in the numerous papers I have cited. My time is up, and I will resume my seat.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
I had hoped that after the urgent appeal from hon. members on this side on Monday night and Tuesday morning, addressed to the Minister of Marine, seeking information on these Estimates, the hon. gentleman, when he rose to-night to take up twenty minutes of the time of the committee, would have endeavoured to throw some light on matters which at present stand in need of explanation. During the time he occupied he took no notice whatever of the representations made by members on this side of the House who, from 12 o'clock on Monday night till 3 o'clock yesterday afternoon, tried their best to elicit some information from the minister. The hon. gentleman tries to make the people believe that members of the Opposition have deliberately attempted to block his Estimates. I do not think that any one can successfully contradict me, however, when I refute that suggestion and say that we on this side have done nothing of the kind. We did try to get certain information to which we are entitled, and which should be given to the committee to enable hon. members to consider the Estimates intelligently; and if the minister had been able or willing to give that information, it would have greatly helped matters and we should have been able to allow him to report progress. However, he did not comply with our request; we got no information of any kind. I do not blame the minister, because, as I pointed out, on different occasions, he has been placed in a very embarrassing position by somebody, whether the Government or the merchant marine people, I do not know. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), has endeavoured to corroborate the statements and the figures of the minister, but I affirm without fear of successful contradiction that no business man in this country, looking over the statements audited and vouched for by Messrs. Marwick, Mitchell



and Company, would regard them as correct. The minister says that these gentlemen are expert accountants. They may be; but these statements which they vouch for are by no means to their credit. I have not sufficient	time to give many
reasons for this assertion, but I may state one. The operating account for 1920 stands:
