These auditors have approved of this statement, but the member for Vancouver Centre, as well as the Minister of Marine, admits that during the year 1920, no interest was paid to the Finance Department by the Canadian Government marine for the money they had borrowed from the Government. I would ask any business man present in this House to-night whether after making up the statement of his affairs at the end of the year, he would not include in the liabilities of the concern, whether an incorporated company or a private business, the interest he owed either to banks, private individuals, or any one else. I submit that when Marwick, Mitchell and Company made up this statement for the Canadian Government marine, and left out of the liabilities the interest that was due the Government for the moneys advanced for construction purposes, they did not make up a correct statement. According to the minister's statement, the vessels which were in commission last year, some 47 in number, cost $50,000,000. Parenthetically, Mr. Chairman, I beg to apologise to the members of the committee for the fact that my voice is somewhat poor to-night; I trust, however, they will bear with me while I try to present my case to the House. Now, if you -figure interest at 51 per cent, which is the amount the Government has to pay for this money, it will mean something like $2,700,000 on this $50,000,000, which the Government 
loaned the merchant marine for the year 1920. Would it not be right, in making up this statement, that this large sum of over $2,000,000 for interest, which the Canadian merchant marine owes the Government, should be included in the liabilities here submitted? But instead of any such sum as $2,700,000 we find in the liability column of operating expenses the small sum of $22,000. The hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) said a moment of two ago that in 1919 the Canadian Government Merchant Marine had in the treasury for the payment of interest the sum of $500,000. Admitting that that is true-although in the statement of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine for 1919 no such amount appears as having been paid-if the hon. gentleman will take his pencil and figure the matter out he will find that instead of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine owing $500,000 for interest in 1919 the sum is nearer $1,250,000. The hon. member shakes his head but let me explain the point to him. It is quite true-as he has no doubt been told-that $25,000,000 were expended in 1919 which would make $1,250,000 interest, but if the hon. member will think for a moment he will realize that not only was money advanced in 1919 but a very large sum was also advanced in 1918, so taking the interest on the money advanced in both these years my figures will be found to be easily within the limit.
There is another point upon which I wish to dwell and it is this: I think it was my genial friend the Minister of Railways who replied to me last year when I asked whether this company would pay a business profits tax to the Government the same as other private companies or corporations would. The Minister of Railways in his genial manner-always anxious to give information and never objecting to do so-said that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, like any other private corporation, would have to pay under the statute a certain amount of money on the profits. Now, Sir, what do we find? That in order to make as good a showing as possible the Canadian Government Merchant Marine presents a statement for 1919 in which they represent that they made a profit of $1,400,000. Of course that profit was only on paper, but they represented it to be the case, and the result is they will have to pay $700,000 as a business profits tax to the Government. That amount has not been paid and consequently the Canadian Government Merchant Marine still

owe that amount to the Government. I say, Sir, that when Messrs. Marwick, Mitchell and Company made up this statement-if they are responsible for it-they should have included in the liabilities of this company not only some $3,000,000 but also $700,000 as the amount of business profits tax payable on the profits of the company in 1919. There are a number of other discrepancies in the statement and I will deal with them in a minute.
The Minister of Marine and the hon. member for Centre Vancouver have again endeavoured to-night to show that the country was behind this project, and that nobody on this side of the House had opposed the building and the operating of ships by the Government. Well, I wish to state that outside of 1918, when the war was on, I have on every occasion objected to the Government entering into the shipbuilding business. When the minister asked us in 1919 for $30,000,000, and again in 1920, when he asked for $20,000,000, I rose in my place and protested against the Government's shipbuilding policy; I told them to sell the ships and clean up the dirty mess as quickly as possible. It is useless for any hon. member opposite now to state that the Opposition were in favour of the Government shipbuilding policy.
Now, Sir, we have asked for certain information. We did so on Monday night and on Tuesday morning. I say that before the Government brought in closure and applied the gag to hon. members on this side, the Minister of Marine should have asked the committee to rise and report progress so that he could obtain the information from Toronto that was asked for. What a spectacle we find presented to us to-night! Yesterday at three o'clock the Prime Minister-who more than anybody else is responsible for the legislation which compels us at 2 o'clock to stop discussing the matter-moved that the committee rise so that the closure motion might be introduced.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
If hon. members opposite
want to cheer they are welcome to do so; but the people of this country who want full information in regard to the operations of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, will not appreciate the fact that the Prime Minister took such a course. And what was one of the excuses advanced by the right hon. gentleman for bringing in the closure motion? Let me recall what he said. At page 2030 of Hansard the Prime
Minister is reported as making this statement :
The hon. member for Red Deer, the hon. member for St. James, Montreal, the hon. member for Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, and the hon. member for Westmoreland all have pleaded for the Government to intervene and have the closure applied in this committee.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I want to state that the hon. member for Lunenburg said no such thing-I want to deny that statement in toto. I do not blame the Prime Minister, because he was not in the House between eleven o"cloek on Monday night and ten o'clock on Tuesday morning, and therefore he did not know whether any one of the hon. gentlemen mentioned asked to have the closure applied. Somebody must have made that statement to my right hon. friend in the endeavour to get the Government out of the hole they were in. Nobody on this side asked for the application of closure. I now see the Prime Minister in his seat and I repeat in his presence the denial I made when he was absent. No such statement as alleged was made by any one of the hon. gentlemen referred to.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
I would ask hon.
gentlemen to please remember that the hon. member for Lunenburg has the floor. He did not rise untli fifteen minutes to two and he is entitled to speak for twenty minutes. Therefore his time has not yet quite expired.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
I certainly believe hon.
members do not wish to gag me and deprive me of this opportunity of stating my position. I was perhaps more interested in the discussion of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine than any other hon. member.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman allow me a question?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Sit down.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
has said that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) did not ask for the closure. Is he quite sure of that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
I was saying that in view
of the fact that I have taken such an interest in this matter and endeavoured to place the facts before the House would, I believed hon. members would give me a little extra time. This important matter, which means the voting of $8,000,000 of the people's money, should not be forced through by closure. If the Opposition had hoen fighting this matter for two, three

or four days, and had been deliberately obstructing, I could understand why the Prime Minister would introduce the closure. But, Sir, we only asked for this information,-I want the Prime Minister to listen to this for a moment-we only asked for this information at twelve o'clock Monday night. The Minister of Marine either refused or would not give that information to us. Under the circumstances the Opposition was perfectly justified in demanding that before the item passed the Minister of Marine should obtain that information from the head office of the Merchant Marine at Toronto and lay it before the committee. Certainly, the Government was not justified in introducing the closure, which debars us tonight from receiving the required information before voting this item of $8,000,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Time:

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
I say the people of this
country will not endorse such drastic measures, and when they are given a chance at the polls, be it sooner or be it later, they will register their protest against the Government in no uncertain manner. When a minister will come before this House and refuse to give the representatives of the people information which they have every right to require, either he should resign his seat or the Government should appeal to the country. Any Government or any party supporting it deserves no credit for such action, and i will be condemned by the people, when the first opportunity offers for an expression of the national will.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: (Translation.) Mr. Chairman, at. this late hour of the night-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: (Translation): I regret it very much, but I cannot let any member have the floor when it is past two o'clock. Unless he was on his feet before two o'clock, no member can speak after two o'clock.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have been on my feet many times before two o'clock and the hon. gentleman who was in the Chair during your absence by acknowledging only the members on the other side was depriving the members on this side of their right to have the floor. Having been on my feet many times before two o'clock, I wish to avail myself of my privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
The ruling of the Chair applies to those who have spoken before two o'clock; it does not apply to the

members who were on their feet but did not catch the eye of the Chairman. I must stand by the ruling that after two o'clock it is utterly impossible, under the rules of this House, to let anybody have the floor.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: May I rise to a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman?

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
The hon. member
could only rise to a question of order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: I think I am quite in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: The hon. member is not in order in rising to a question of privilege after two o'clock when the vote is before the House. He would be in order in rising to a point of order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: May I rise to a point of order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: My point of order is this: I did not have an opportunity to speak on this debate after the Prime Minister misinformed the committee as to something which I was supposed to have said, but which I never said at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Order, order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext: Before this motion is put I think I should be allowed to rise to a question of privilege to correct the Prime Minister. I am not very much concerned about correcting him, but I wish to inform the committee as to a false impression that the Prime Minister conveyed, something that he does very often.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
In deciding the point of order, I must tell the hon. member that the fact that he rose and was unable to be recognized by the Chair before two o'clock does not give him the right at the present time to make any correction whatsoever. I regret the hon. member was not seen by the Chair when he rose to address the committee. That, however, is his misfortune, and the rule must be followed.
The question is now on item 218. Sir Henry Drayton moves:
That a sum not exceeding $8,330,000 be placed at the disposal of His Majesty for a Government shipbuilding programme, being the amount required for the construction of the vessels in accordance with the said Government programme.
Motion agreed to on division: yeas, 103; nays, 79.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
Sir Henry Drayton moves:
That a sum of money not exceeding $71,499,703.70, being one-sixth of the amount of each of the several items set forth in the Main Estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1922, and one-sixth of the amount of the item for a provisional bonus allowance for the inside and outside services of the Civil Service set forth in the Supplementary Estimate for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1922, be granted to His Majesty for the fiscal year ending the March 31, 1922.
Mr. Lemieux moves in amendment:
That the total amount mentioned in the resolution be reduced by the sum of $13,407.16, being one-sixth, of the amount of item No. 325 for salaries and contingencies of the Purchasing Commission and that said Item be not included in the schedule to said resolution.
The question is on the amendment.
Amendment negatived on division: yeas, 77; nays, 103.
Mr.vMIDDLEBRO:	Mr. Chairman, I
would call attention to the fact that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) is in his seat and has not voted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-RECIPROCITY AMENDMENT MOVED BY HON. ME. FIELDING
speechtext:
I must point out to the hon. member for Grey that in committee an hon. member is not obliged to vote. The question is on the main motion.
Main motion (Sir Henry Drayton) agreed to; yeas, 117; nays, 63.
Resolutions reported and concurred in.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of Sir Henry Drayton, the House went into Committee of Ways and Means, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL
speechtext: Resolved, That towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty on account of certain expenses of the Public Service for the financial year ending March 31, 1922, the sum of $71,499,703.70 be granted out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Sir HENRY DRAYTON thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 42, for granting to His Majesty certain sums of money for the public service for the financial year ending March 31, 1922.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
On motion of Right Hon. Mr. Meighen for the adjournment of the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL
speechtext: What business does the Government intend to take up later on in the day?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL
speechtext: Chiefly Supply.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL
speechtext: What Supply?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL
speechtext: We are ready for all Supply now, except that we will not go into External Affairs. Probably Government Orders will be taken up too. They are all on the Order Paper. I do not know of any specially.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and the House adjourned at 2.25 a.m. Thursday.
Thursday, April 14, 1921
